extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of humor theory, literary critics, and psychologists
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and using historical and theoretical criteria for explaining, classifying, or evaluating comic experience and humorous writing/performances. Emphasizes classical and modern theories of causes and functions of laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modulation between humor and pathos
rubrics_metrics.description: “For his humor is not so far out of key with pathos as to be destroyed by their modulation the one into the other. It is a modulation between serious and playful pain — a thing which seems to enhance, almost as though with a tremor of peril, our enjoyment of them both.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good humor can sit close to pathos and shift into it without losing value; the interplay of seriousness and playfully painful feeling can heighten both comic and tragic effects. Example: the Tommy episodes (boy returning to mother; buying Byron picture) that make readers 'not know whether to laugh or cry.' Anti-pattern: humor that is so flippant it obliterates pathos.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vulnerability to flippancy (avoid the 'Smart Aleck')
rubrics_metrics.description: “Pathos is impossible to the flippant; in their very presence its color blanches ... Both for the purposes of joy and sorrow, therefore, we resist them.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humor that aims to include pathos must resist superficial, fresh, or flipant jokery. Flippant remarks destroy the capacity for mixed feelings; protect the integrity of pathos by avoiding glibness or gratuitous wit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two kinds of laughter / mixture of satisfaction and disappointment
rubrics_metrics.description: “Their explanations divide themselves into three classes — those which seek the cause of laughter in some kind of disappointment, those which seek it in some kind of satisfaction, and those which seek it in a mixture of satisfaction with disappointment.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comprehensive accounts of comic experience often require combining at least two general moods (satisfaction/pleasure and disappointment/pain). When analyzing jokes, consider whether they appeal to surprise (disappointment of expectation), to gratification, or to both together.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derision / pleasure in others' humiliation (Plato)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plato: laughter as “an enjoyment of other people’s misfortunes” (pleasure of seeing others humiliated); author notes Plato should have used 'pity' rather than 'envy'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One historical criterion: comic pleasure may derive from perceiving others as humiliated/stupid. Critical note: this account can be improved by acknowledging pity or imaginative presence rather than mere envy. Watch for ethical implications when evaluating humor that targets individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic as ugliness that is not harmful (Aristotle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle defined the occasion of comic laughter as 'an ugliness that is not harmful' — 'some defect or ugliness which is not painful or destructive.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comic material often involves a defect, distortion, or ugliness that stops short of real harm; when evaluating comic subjects, ensure the 'ugliness' is harmless rather than injurious. Examples: comic masks, exaggerated traits. Anti-pattern: real suffering presented as comic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joke as deceived expectation / surprise (Aristotle in Rhetoric)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle in the Rhetoric: identifies a joke with a deceived expectation — enjoying what 'is stated which we did not expect, and we acknowledge it to be true.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A central formal device for producing laughter is violating anticipations: set up an expectation, then subvert it in a way the audience recognizes as true or fitting. Use surprise and reversal of expectation; watch that the punchline registers as both unexpected and intelligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of truth in the unexpected (Isocrates example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Isocrates' pun: sovereignty/beginning -> 'the sovereignty of the Athenians was the beginning of their troubles' — we enjoy it because 'that is stated which we did not expect, and we acknowledge it to be true.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humor can arise when an unexpected formulation nonetheless reveals a truth; the cognitive pleasure comes from sudden recognition. When crafting or evaluating a joke, consider whether the surprise also yields insight or aptness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy as sociability and revelry (origins)
rubrics_metrics.description: The comic's origins in 'village revelry or merrymaking' — comedy as Pantagruellian, mirthful, sexual, social, convivial rather than primarily scornful or intellectual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't reduce comedy to scorn or lampoonry; evaluate many comic works by their sociable, communal, celebratory features (farce, tomfoolery, conviviality). Consider tone, warmth, and inclusiveness as positive comic qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughter as rhetorical instrument (Cicero)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cicero: it is part of the orator’s business to raise a laugh because it 'lessens, confounds, hampers, frightens, and confutes the opponent.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humor can be judged by its effectiveness as a persuasive or disruptive tool in rhetoric: does it deflate an opponent or clarify a position? Ethical caution: use of ridicule as a rhetorical weapon can be morally fraught.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-directed laughter when expectation deceives (Cicero / Lamennais)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cicero's reconciliation: when laughter arises from deceived expectation 'our mistake makes us laugh at ourselves.' Lamennais: pride admires itself for not being a dupe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Genial humor often targets the self or shared human foibles; evaluate whether laughter is compassionate/self-aware versus derisive. Self-mockery is often a sign of genial humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derision theory (Hobbes): 'sudden glory' and superiority
rubrics_metrics.description: Hobbes: 'Sudden glory is the passion which maketh those Grimaces called Laughter' — caused by sudden self-applauding comparison or perceiving deformity in another; much laughter at others' defects is a sign of pusillanimity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This influential historical criterion locates comic pleasure in felt superiority. When assessing humor, consider whether it depends on elevating the laughers over targets. Critical note: such laughter may indicate smallness of mind or cruelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstracted absurdity (Hobbes' qualification)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hobbes' further claim: 'Laughter without offense must be at absurdities and infirmities abstracted from persons.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To avoid malice, comedy can target abstract absurdities or behaviors rather than people. Evaluate whether the joke abstracts the fault (acceptable) or personalizes it (potentially offensive).

rubrics_metrics.name: Derision mixed with hate and surprise (Descartes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Descartes: 'Derision or mockery is a kind of joy mixed with hate ... when that happens unexpectedly, the surprise is the cause of our bursting out laughing.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some theories see derision allied to moral judgment: laughter may involve a feeling that someone deserves the misfortune. When evaluating, note the moral tint (justice/hatred) in the laugher's response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-phase comic process (Zeising)
rubrics_metrics.description: Zeising: comic process has three phases — (1) a shock from an object that seems to be something and yet is not, (2) a counter-shock freeing us from deception and recognizing nothingness, (3) our happy sense of superiority to that nothingness which makes us laugh.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze jokes as sequences: initial deception, revelation, and resultant feeling of playful superiority. This helps explain why surprise alone is not sufficient; the perceptual 'correction' matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inward imitation / aesthetic participation (Karl Groos)
rubrics_metrics.description: Groos: during the second phase there is a moment of 'inward imitation' of the absurdity; aesthetic perception involves 'transporting of oneself into the object' before emerging laughing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affective participation in the absurd — briefly sharing the object's perspective — can deepen comic pleasure and make laughter aesthetically pleasurable rather than merely scornful. Good humor may invite the audience into the absurdity rather than only mock it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Playful scorn and slight misfortune (Ziegler / Groos)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ziegler: we laugh at the stupidities and misfortunes of others only when they are slight and inconsequential, and our scorn is essentially playful. Groos uses 'fighting-play' to qualify playful derision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether the harm made comic is genuinely slight and safely within 'play' — larger harms are inappropriate subjects for mirth. Playful scorn is acceptable when it remains benign and mutual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature's derision / limits revealed (Stephan Schiitze)
rubrics_metrics.description: Schiitze: we laugh because nature derides us by bringing our intended sublimities to a fall, showing the limits of our freedom — we enjoy perceiving that 'she is playing a game!'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some comic responses come from recognizing human limitations exposed by circumstance. Evaluate jokes that reveal the gap between intention and outcome as comic in a way that is cosmically impersonal rather than malicious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teasing as fundamental; objective vs subjective comic (Otto Schauer)
rubrics_metrics.description: Schauer: 'Teasing is a game in which the players take the role of adversaries.' He divides comic experience into objective-comic (jokes in which we triumph) and subjective-comic (jokes in which we are triumphed over).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider humor as interactive play involving role-taking; classify jokes by whether the audience/characters are placed in triumph or defeat. Evaluate whether the teasing remains playful and consensual (healthy) or becomes hostile (unhealthy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor as a device / consolation not substitute for life
rubrics_metrics.description: “Humor is a most adroit and exquisite device by which our nerves outwit the stings and paltry bitterness of life, but it is after all only a device. It cannot be substituted for life... His sense of humor is more rich than consolation, but it is not victory.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat humor as a valuable but limited response to life's pains: it consoles and reframes but does not replace engagement with serious realities. In evaluation, distinguish between humor that enlightens/reconciles and humor that merely avoids or trivializes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skeptical/agnostic stance: humor resists rigorous definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors (Cicero, Hume, Croce, Cazamian, Ribot, Dugas) and experiments (Hall's questionnaire) conclude that laughter's occasions are enormously varied and that 'humor escapes science' or 'we cannot define humor' in a single rigorous way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodological caution: avoid forcing a single universal definition or checklist onto humor. When evaluating or theorizing, allow for multiple legitimate types and combine frameworks rather than insisting on one master explanation.
